dash.dimension_help: Normalised score: 0 = historical average, ±1 = one standard deviation.
dash.states_rule: **The rule** labels each day from the three scores: **Stress / crisis** if stress is above {stress_threshold}; otherwise **Inflationary overheating** if inflation is above {inflation_threshold}; otherwise **Slowdown** if growth is below {growth_threshold}; otherwise **Expansion**.
dash.states_help: The model ({model}) groups days into states that have no name. Each state takes the name of the regime whose **centre** is closest to its own, a regime's centre being the average day the rule puts in that regime over the training period. Nothing is set by hand: two states can share a name, and a regime absent from history cannot name any state. The table shows the fit used on this date and the share of each state's days that the rule puts in the regime it is named after (agreement).
dash.states_none: This model predicts the rule regimes directly: it has no states to name.
dash.states_shares: How each state's training days split across the rule regimes. A state under 50% is a mixed state.
dash.states_cube: The three dimensions together: one dot every 5 days, colored by the rule regime; numbered diamonds = centres of the model's states; large dot = date shown.

method.text: Data is turned into 12 point-in-time indicators (rolling windows, z-scores on the history available at each date, publication lags for monthly series), grouped into three dimensions: stress, growth, inflation. A transparent rule defines the 4 regimes from these three scores. The default model combines a statistical jump model (persistent regimes, causal filtering), whose states each take the name of the closest regime centre, with two fast models that raise the stress probability (gradient boosting one week ahead, stress-onset detector). The stress probability shown is calibrated: a small logistic regression (Platt scaling), refitted on past days only, turns the highest stress reading into how often stress actually followed. The stress alarm reads the uncalibrated detector score, tuned for speed. Every probability shown is out of sample (walk-forward). Stress episodes are dated by a rule fixed before testing.

world.method: How the stress state is computed
world.method_text: This is not the macro regime (stress, growth, inflation), which exists only for the United States. For each country, from its ETF alone: **Stress** when 21-day realised volatility is in the top {stress_pct}% of its last 5 years **and** the drawdown from the 1-year high is beyond {dd}; **Elevated** when volatility is in the top {elevated_pct}%; **Calm** otherwise. A new state counts after {days} days in a row. Same thresholds for every country, set before looking at real data, computed only from data available each day.

tr.live.title: Live record
tr.live.intro: Published every business day after the US close by an automated job, from data available that evening, before anyone knows what comes next. Each day is a JSON file chained to the day before by its SHA-256 hash and stamped with OpenTimestamps, which anchors that hash in the Bitcoin blockchain. A day cannot be edited, deleted or backdated without it showing below.

tr.live.crises_help: Dated afterwards by the frozen episode rule on market data; each latency is measured against the alarm exactly as it was published that evening, never recomputed.
tr.live.no_crisis: No stress episode dated by the frozen rule between {start} and {end}.
tr.live.alarms: Every alarm since the live start
tr.verify.title: Check it yourself
tr.verify.intro: Download a day's .json and .json.ots files from the table (or from track_record/ in the repository), then:
tr.verify.c1: the sha256 of that day in index.csv
tr.verify.c2: needs pip install opentimestamps-client; prints the Bitcoin block and its date
tr.verify.outro: Each file also holds previous_sha256, the hash of the day before, so changing one day breaks every later one. A fresh proof is "pending" for a few hours, until a Bitcoin block confirms it; the daily job then completes it. Git commit dates are shown nowhere on this page: they can be rewritten, the Bitcoin anchor cannot.

Read it as evidence of what the method does; the live record above is the proof.

tr.method.title: Method and limits
tr.method.text:
What is measured. A stress episode starts when US equities (SPY) fall {dd} from their 1-year high or when their volatility breaks above its historical {q}th percentile. This rule was frozen on 2026-10-01 before any result was seen; its SHA-256 is printed in every published day, and the code refuses to run with any other version.

The alarm turns on when the detector score stays above {thr} for {n} days. P(stress) is a separate, calibrated number: when it says 30%, stress followed about 3 times in 10 in the past. The alarm is tuned for speed, the probability for honesty.

Limits. A dozen or so crises since 2009 are few, and the median moves a lot with one of them. Negative delays mean the alarm was already on, not that the crisis was foreseen. The detector watches the same market the rule dates episodes on, so a delay near zero means "on the day it started". Market prices are not published here (data licences): only the model's outputs, episode dates and drawdowns.

Full method and every pre-registered decision: detection, calibration, publication.

learn.fed.how_beginner: Where do these odds come from?
learn.fed.how_beginner_text: Short-term US government bonds (Treasury bills) pay an interest rate close to what investors expect the Fed's rate to be over the next months. If a 3-month bill pays more than today's Fed rate, investors expect a hike; if it pays less, a cut. We turn that gap into odds. It is an approximation from free public data, not the official futures-based odds (CME FedWatch), which are licensed and cannot be shown here.

learn.lab.bond: 💵 What happens to a bond when rates move?
learn.lab.bond_help.beginner: When interest rates go up, existing bonds lose value, and long bonds lose more. That is what hurt banks like SVB in 2023.
learn.lab.bond_help.pro: Annual-coupon bond repriced exactly; modified duration D and convexity C by finite differences. ΔP/P ≈ -D·Δy + ½·C·Δy².
learn.lab.curve: 🔮 Recession odds from the yield curve
learn.lab.curve_help.beginner: When short rates are above long rates (an inverted curve), a recession has often followed within a year or two. This simple model turns the gap into a probability.
learn.lab.curve_help.pro: New York Fed probit (Estrella and Trubin 2006): P(recession in 12 months) = Φ(-0.5333 - 0.6330 × spread), spread = 10y - 3m in points. Fitted on 1959-2006; 2022-24 was a false alarm so far.
learn.lab.curve_chart_help: The model's probability each month (monthly average spread) and the recessions that followed (grey).

learn.lab.ppower_help.pro: CPI-U (CPIAUCSL) ratio, mid-year of the start year to the analysis date. CPI overstates the cost of living somewhat (substitution and quality bias, Boskin 1996).

learn.lab.wage_real: Real change in what you can buy
learn.lab.wage_help.beginner: Prefilled with average US hourly earnings growth and CPI inflation. If prices rise faster than pay, you can buy less even with a raise.
learn.lab.wage_help.pro: (1 + w) / (1 + π) - 1 with average hourly earnings (CES0500000003) and CPI-U; composition effects bias average earnings up in recessions (2020).
learn.lab.debt_help.beginner: Debt grows with deficits and with interest, but the economy grows too. If the economy grows faster than the interest rate, debt is easier to carry.
learn.lab.debt_help.pro: d(t+1) = d(t)·(1 + r)/(1 + g) + primary deficit, nominal r (average interest on debt) and g (nominal GDP growth). Stabilising primary balance = d·(r - g)/(1 + g). Start prefilled with federal debt to GDP (GFDEGDQ188S).
learn.lab.debt_deficit: Primary deficit (% of GDP, before interest)
learn.lab.debt_rate: Interest rate paid on the debt (%)
learn.lab.debt_stabilise: Primary balance that keeps debt flat
